decks.title: Aids to Health — Part 1: Vaccines, antitoxins, serums and antibiotics
goals: Explain how a vaccine produces immunity and distinguish vaccination from immunisation
Explain when an antitoxin or serum is given instead of a vaccine
State what antibiotics act against and why they must be used carefully

slides.heading: Aids to Health
slides.body_md: Part 1 — medicines and injections that protect us from germs.

visual.alt: Flow from germs entering the body to antibodies being made and a memory remaining

slides.narration: Our body can fight germs on its own, and we can help it. Vaccines train the body before the germs arrive. Serums give ready-made help in an emergency. Antibiotics kill bacteria. In this part we learn when each one is used.

slides.heading: How the body fights a germ

rows: A germ, or part of a germ, that the body treats as foreign
A protein made by white blood cells that fights one kind of germ
White blood cells that remember a germ, so that the next attack is met quickly
Resistance of the body to a disease

visual.alt: Table of the terms antigen, antibody, memory cells and immunity with their meanings

slides.narration: When a germ enters the body, white blood cells make antibodies against it. Some of these cells remain as memory cells. If the same germ comes again, the body answers quickly. This resistance is called immunity.

slides.heading: What a vaccine is

rows: Too weak to cause the disease
A harmless form of a poison made by the germ
It cannot poison, but the body still makes antibodies
A harmless part of the germ

visual.alt: Table of the kinds of material in a vaccine and why each is safe

slides.narration: A vaccine is made from weakened germs, killed germs, a harmless form of a germ poison or a harmless part of a germ. It cannot cause the disease, yet it makes the body produce antibodies and memory cells. So the body is ready before the real germ comes.

slides.heading: Antibodies after a first dose and a booster
slides.body_md: A second dose, a **booster**, gives a faster and higher response.

slides.body_md: A vaccine protects a person because it makes the body produce
slides.narration: The body prepares before the real germ arrives.

slides.heading: Vaccination and immunisation

rows: Giving a vaccine to a person, by injection or by drops in the mouth
The process by which a person becomes immune to a disease
The result, or the whole process
Yes, it is the giving of a vaccine
No; immunity may also come from ready-made antibodies or from having the disease
A child is given drops against polio
The child is now protected against polio

visual.alt: Table distinguishing vaccination from immunisation by meaning, nature, use of a vaccine and example

slides.narration: Vaccination means giving a vaccine. Immunisation is the process by which the person becomes immune. Vaccination is the method, and immunisation is the result. A person can also become immune by being given ready-made antibodies.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: reading the booster graph
slides.body_md: First dose on day 0, booster on day 28. The highest level after the first dose is 8 on day 14; after the booster it is 72 on day 35. How many times higher is the second peak, and how many times sooner was it reached?
bullets: Step 1: height ratio = 72 ÷ 8 = **9** times higher.
Step 2: time to first peak = 14 days; time to second peak = 35 − 28 = **7** days.
Step 3: 14 ÷ 7 = **2** times sooner. The memory cells made the faster, stronger response.

visual.alt: Worked table comparing the highest antibody level and the days taken after the first dose and the booster

slides.narration: Divide the second peak by the first. Seventy-two divided by eight is nine, so nine times higher. The first peak took fourteen days. The second took only seven days after the booster, which is twice as fast. Memory cells explain both.

slides.heading: Diseases for which vaccines are given

rows: A vaccine is given to infants
Given as drops in the mouth or by injection
Often given together in one injection

visual.alt: Table of diseases for which vaccines are given, with cause and note

slides.narration: Vaccines are given against many diseases. These include tuberculosis, polio, measles, hepatitis B, and diphtheria, whooping cough and tetanus together. The exact schedule of doses is decided by health authorities and is updated from time to time.

slides.heading: Antitoxins and serums

rows: An antibody that neutralises a poison made by germs
The clear part of blood holding ready-made antibodies
From an immunised animal or person
From an immunised animal, often a horse, or from a recovered person
To treat diphtheria or tetanus after the poison is already at work
When quick help is needed, or for a bite or sting, or after exposure
A short time, because the body made no antibodies of its own

visual.alt: Table comparing antitoxin and serum by what they are, source, use and length of protection

slides.narration: An antitoxin neutralises the poison made by germs. A serum is the part of blood with ready-made antibodies, often taken from an immunised horse. They work at once, but only for a short time, because the person has not made antibodies himself.

slides.heading: Quick check: ready-made help
slides.body_md: A person who has already been exposed to dangerous germs needs protection at once. The best choice is
slides.narration: A vaccine needs days to work.

slides.heading: Why a serum, not a vaccine, in an emergency

rows: After exposure or in an emergency

visual.alt: Table comparing a vaccine with a serum or antitoxin by speed, antibodies, memory and best use

slides.narration: A vaccine makes the body build its own antibodies, which takes days or weeks, but the protection lasts long. A serum gives antibodies at once but they fade soon. So a vaccine is for prevention and a serum is for an emergency.

slides.heading: Antibiotics

rows: Chemicals made by living things such as moulds and bacteria, now also made in factories
Bacteria; they do not act on viruses
Only on a doctor's advice, in the right dose, for the full course
Bacteria become resistant; useful bacteria in the gut are killed; some people are allergic

visual.alt: Table of what antibiotics are, what they act against, examples and care in their use

slides.narration: Antibiotics kill bacteria or stop them from growing. They do not act on viruses, so they do not help against a cold. They should be taken only on a doctor's advice and for the full course. Misuse makes bacteria resistant.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: stopping the course too early
slides.body_md: A doctor prescribes 3 tablets a day for 10 days. The patient feels better and stops after 4 days. What percentage of the course is left untaken?
bullets: Step 1: full course = 3 × 10 = **30** tablets.
Step 3: left = 18 ÷ 30 × 100 = **60 per cent**. Some bacteria may survive and become resistant.

visual.alt: Worked table: thirty tablets in the course, twelve taken, eighteen left, sixty per cent

slides.narration: The full course is three tablets a day for ten days, which is thirty tablets. After four days the patient has taken twelve, so eighteen are left. That is sixty per cent of the course. The bacteria that survive may become resistant.

slides.heading: Quick check: what antibiotics act on
slides.body_md: Antibiotics are useful against diseases caused by
slides.narration: A cold and influenza are not in this group.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Vaccine: harmless germ material; the body makes antibodies and memory cells; long protection.
Vaccination is giving the vaccine; immunisation is becoming immune.
Antitoxin and serum: ready-made help for an emergency; short protection.
Antibiotics act on bacteria, not viruses; take the full course on a doctor's advice.

visual.alt: Summary table of vaccine, serum or antitoxin and antibiotic by when they act and how long they protect

slides.narration: To recap. A vaccine trains the body and gives long protection. Vaccination is the giving, and immunisation is becoming immune. Serums and antitoxins give ready-made help for a short time. Antibiotics act on bacteria and must be taken for the full course.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Say that a vaccine makes the body **produce its own antibodies** and **memory cells**.
Say that a **serum gives ready-made antibodies**, so it works **at once** but only **for a short time**.
Do not write that antibiotics act on **viruses**.
Give a **reason** for finishing the course: surviving bacteria may become **resistant**.
slides.narration: Exam tips. For a vaccine, say that the body makes its own antibodies and memory cells. For a serum, say that the antibodies are ready-made, so it acts at once but only for a short time. Antibiotics do not act on viruses. Finish the course to avoid resistance.

decks.title: Aids to Health — Part 2: Antiseptics, disinfectants, local defences and health organisations
goals: Distinguish antiseptics from disinfectants with examples
Describe the first-line defences of the body and their merits
List the major activities of the Red Cross and the World Health Organization

slides.heading: Keeping Germs Out
slides.body_md: Part 2 — chemicals that clean, the body's own defences, and organisations that look after health.

visual.alt: Flow from chemicals through the body defences to health organisations

slides.narration: Besides vaccines and antibiotics, we use chemicals to destroy germs outside the body. Our body also has its own defences that work all the time. Finally, we look at two organisations that work for health around the world.

slides.heading: Antiseptics

rows: Mild chemicals that kill germs or stop them from growing
Living tissue: cuts, wounds, skin and hands
A strong chemical would damage the living cells
Dilute hydrogen peroxide, tincture of iodine, boric acid, antiseptic creams and soaps

visual.alt: Table of what antiseptics are, where they are used, why they are mild and examples

slides.narration: Antiseptics are mild chemicals that kill germs or stop them growing. They are used on living tissue such as cuts, wounds and hands. They must be mild, or they would harm living cells. Dilute hydrogen peroxide and boric acid are examples.

slides.heading: Disinfectants

rows: Non-living things: floors, drains, toilets, clothes and instruments
They are strong enough to harm living cells
Phenyl floor cleaner, bleaching powder, formalin, chlorine tablets in water

visual.alt: Table of what disinfectants are, where they are used, why not on skin and examples

slides.narration: Disinfectants are strong chemicals that kill germs on things that are not alive, such as floors, drains and instruments. They are too strong to be used on the skin. Phenyl, bleaching powder and chlorine are examples.

slides.heading: Antiseptic, disinfectant and antibiotic compared

visual.alt: Table comparing antiseptic, disinfectant and antibiotic by use, strength, action and example

slides.narration: An antiseptic is mild and used on living tissue outside the body. A disinfectant is strong and used on things that are not alive. An antibiotic is taken inside the body and acts on bacteria. Each has its own place.

slides.heading: Quick check: for a floor
slides.body_md: A chemical that is strong enough to clean a hospital floor but would harm the skin is a
slides.narration: It is used on things that are not alive.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: making an antiseptic solution
slides.body_md: A nurse mixes 20 mL of an antiseptic concentrate with 180 mL of clean water. What is the volume of the solution and its strength in per cent?
bullets: Step 1: volume = 20 + 180 = **200 mL**.
Step 2: strength = 20 ÷ 200 × 100 = **10 per cent**.
Step 3: diluting makes it **mild enough** for living tissue.

visual.alt: Worked table: twenty millilitres of concentrate in two hundred millilitres gives a ten per cent solution

slides.narration: Add the two volumes. Twenty plus one hundred eighty gives two hundred millilitres. The concentrate is twenty out of two hundred, which is ten per cent. Dilution makes the solution mild enough to use on a wound.

slides.heading: The first line of defence
slides.body_md: Many barriers keep germs out before any medicine is needed.

slides.narration: The body has barriers all over. The skin is a tough covering. Tears and saliva wash the eyes and mouth. The nose and windpipe trap germs in mucus. Acid in the stomach kills many germs that are swallowed.

slides.heading: First-line defences of the body

rows: The horny layer is a tough barrier; oil and sweat make the surface unfriendly to germs
Mucus and hairs in the nose
Trap dust and germs before they reach the lungs
Hair-like structures that sweep mucus with trapped germs up to the throat
Wash the surface and hold an enzyme that kills many bacteria
Kills most germs that are swallowed with food and water

visual.alt: Table of the first-line defences of the body and how each works

slides.narration: The skin is a barrier. Mucus and hairs in the nose trap dust and germs. Cilia in the windpipe sweep the mucus upward. Tears and saliva wash and kill bacteria. Stomach acid kills germs that are swallowed. Sneezing and coughing blow them out.

slides.body_md: Mucus catches germs, and the **cilia** sweep it upward.

sections.heading: 1. Vaccination and immunisation
sections.body_md:
**How the body fights a germ.** A germ, or a part of it, that the body treats as foreign is an **antigen**. White blood cells make **antibodies** against it. Some of these cells stay as **memory cells**, so that a second attack is met faster and more strongly. Resistance to a disease is called **immunity**.

**A vaccine** is a preparation that makes the body produce antibodies and memory cells **without causing the disease**. It may contain:
- **weakened** living germs,
- **killed** germs,
- a harmless form of a **poison (toxin)** made by the germ, or
- a harmless **part** of the germ.

A **booster dose** (a later second dose) works faster and gives a much higher antibody level because of the memory cells (see the graph).

| | **Vaccination** | **Immunisation** |
|---|---|---|
| Meaning | **Giving** a vaccine (by injection or drops) | The **process of becoming immune** to a disease |
| Nature | The method | The result (or the whole process) |
| Vaccine always used? | Yes | No: immunity can also come from ready-made antibodies |

Vaccines are given against tuberculosis, polio, measles, diphtheria, whooping cough, tetanus and hepatitis B, among others. Vaccines **prevent** disease; they give **active** immunity that lasts long. The exact schedule of doses is decided by health authorities and is revised from time to time (as of 2026); schedules are not part of this syllabus.

Textbooks sometimes use the two words "vaccination" and "immunisation" almost as one; for an examination, give the distinction above.

key_terms.definition_md: A preparation that makes the body make antibodies without causing the disease.
A protein made by white blood cells that fights one kind of germ.
A later dose of a vaccine that gives a faster and higher response.
The process by which a person becomes immune to a disease.

sections.heading: 2. Antitoxins, serums and antibiotics
sections.body_md:
**Antitoxin:** an antibody that **neutralises a poison (toxin)** made by germs, for example in diphtheria or tetanus. **Serum:** the clear part of blood that holds **ready-made antibodies**, taken from an immunised animal (often a horse) or from a person who has recovered. Serums are also used for animal bites and stings.

**Why a serum instead of a vaccine?** A vaccine makes the body build its own antibodies, which takes days or weeks. A person who has already been exposed, or who is already ill and needs help at once, is given ready-made antibodies.

| | **Vaccine** | **Serum or antitoxin** |
|---|---|---|
| Gives | The germ made harmless | Ready-made antibodies |
| Body makes antibodies? | Yes | No |
| Speed | Slow | Immediate |
| Memory cells | Yes | No |
| Protection | Long | Short |
| Best used | Before exposure | After exposure, or in an emergency |

**Antibiotics** are chemicals made by living things such as moulds and bacteria (many are now made in factories) that **kill bacteria or stop their growth**. Examples: penicillin, streptomycin, tetracycline. They **do not act on viruses**, so they do not help against a cold, influenza or chicken pox.

**Use carefully:** only on a doctor's advice, in the correct dose, and for the **full course**. Misuse allows bacteria to become **resistant**, kills useful bacteria in the gut and may cause allergies.

key_terms.definition_md: An antibody that neutralises a toxin made by germs.
The part of blood that holds ready-made antibodies.
A chemical that kills bacteria or stops their growth.
The ability of bacteria to survive an antibiotic.

sections.heading: 3. Antiseptics and disinfectants
sections.body_md:
| | **Antiseptic** | **Disinfectant** |
|---|---|---|
| Strength | **Mild** | **Strong** |
| Used on | **Living tissue**: cuts, wounds, skin, hands | **Non-living things**: floors, drains, toilets, instruments, clothes |
| Why | Must not damage living cells | Too strong for living tissue |
| Examples | Dilute hydrogen peroxide, tincture of iodine, boric acid, antiseptic soaps and creams | Phenyl floor cleaner, bleaching powder, formalin, chlorine tablets |

The same chemical may act as an antiseptic when **dilute** and as a disinfectant when **strong**; this is why the dilution matters. Antiseptics and disinfectants are used **outside** the body and act on many kinds of germs. **Antibiotics** are taken **inside** the body and act on bacteria only.

key_terms.definition_md: A mild chemical that kills germs or stops their growth and is safe on living tissue.
A strong chemical used to kill germs on non-living things.

sections.heading: 4. The body's local defence system and its merits
sections.body_md:
The first line of defence stops germs from getting in.

| Defence | How it works |
|---|---|
| **Skin** | The horny layer is a tough, waterproof barrier; oil and sweat make the surface unfriendly to germs |
| **Mucus and hairs in the nose** | Trap dust and germs before they reach the lungs |
| **Cilia in the windpipe** | Hair-like structures that sweep mucus with trapped germs up to the throat, where it is swallowed or coughed out |
| **Tears and saliva** | Wash the surface and contain an enzyme that kills many bacteria |
| **Acid in the stomach** | Kills most germs swallowed with food and water |
| **Sneezing and coughing** | Blow out germs and dust |

**Merits:** the defences are **immediate** (always in place), **general** (they act against all kinds of germs), **natural** (no injection or medicine) and **protective** (they stop most germs from entering at all). Germs that pass these barriers are met by white blood cells and antibodies (the second line, not part of this chapter).

key_terms.definition_md: A sticky fluid that traps dust and germs.
Tiny hair-like structures that beat to sweep mucus along.
The barriers that keep germs out of the body.

sections.heading: 5. Health organisations: the Red Cross and the WHO
sections.body_md:
**The Red Cross** (a world-wide movement; in India, the Indian Red Cross Society)
- Started by **Henry Dunant** after he saw the suffering of wounded soldiers in a battle; the movement began in **1863**.
- Emblem: a **red cross on a white background**.
- Aim: to protect life and health and to relieve suffering, without taking sides.
- **Major activities:** first aid and ambulance service; relief to the victims of wars, floods, earthquakes and other disasters (food, shelter, blankets, medical care); **blood donation camps and blood banks**; training in first aid, nursing and health; care of the wounded and of prisoners of war; helping to trace missing family members.

**The World Health Organization (WHO)**
- The **health agency of the United Nations**, with its headquarters in **Geneva**; founded in **1948** (World Health Day is on 7 April).
- Aim: the **highest possible level of health for all people**.
- **Major activities:** fighting communicable diseases and running immunisation drives (it announced the worldwide end of smallpox in 1980); responding to epidemics; **research** and sharing health information; setting **standards** for medicines and food; **training** health workers; promoting clean water, sanitation, nutrition and mother and child health.

Details of current programmes, the number of member countries and the policies of both bodies change with time; only stable points are in this chapter (as of 2026).

key_terms.definition_md: A movement that gives relief, first aid and care in wars and disasters.
The World Health Organization, the health agency of the United Nations.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Writing that a vaccine gives **ready-made antibodies**; that is a **serum**.
- Saying antibiotics cure **viral** diseases such as a cold or influenza.
- Confusing **antiseptic** (mild, living tissue) with **disinfectant** (strong, non-living things).
- Leaving out **memory cells** when explaining how a vaccine gives long protection.
- Mixing up the activities of the **Red Cross** (relief, first aid, blood banks) and the **WHO** (disease control, standards, research).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1 mark: a term, an odd one out **with its category**, a give-reason item.
- 2 marks: two points, one use and one example, or a difference.
- 3 marks: a three-row comparison, three defences with their role, or three activities.
- 10-mark structured question: a short situation or diagram with parts of 2 to 4 marks; one part is a labelled diagram.

cards.back_md: A protein made by white blood cells that fights one kind of germ.
White blood cells that remember a germ so that the next attack is met quickly.
A preparation that makes the body make antibodies without causing the disease.

cards.front_md: Four kinds of material in vaccines?
cards.back_md: Weakened germs, killed germs, harmless toxin, harmless part of a germ.
A later dose of a vaccine that gives a faster and higher response.
The giving of a vaccine to a person.
The process by which a person becomes immune to a disease.

cards.front_md: Does a vaccine give long or short protection?
cards.back_md: Long, because memory cells are formed.

cards.front_md: Name two diseases for which vaccines are given.
cards.back_md: Tuberculosis, polio, measles, hepatitis B, tetanus (any two).
An antibody that neutralises a toxin made by germs.
The part of blood that holds ready-made antibodies.

cards.front_md: Where does a serum often come from?
cards.back_md: An immunised animal such as a horse, or a recovered person.

cards.front_md: Why is a serum used instead of a vaccine in an emergency?
cards.back_md: It gives ready-made antibodies at once; a vaccine takes days or weeks.

cards.front_md: How long does a serum protect?
cards.back_md: Only a short time; the body makes no memory cells.
Chemicals that kill bacteria or stop their growth.
Penicillin, streptomycin, tetracycline (any two).
No, only on bacteria.

cards.front_md: Why take the full course of an antibiotic?
cards.back_md: Surviving bacteria may become resistant.
Bacteria become resistant; useful gut bacteria are killed; allergy.
A mild chemical used on living tissue to kill germs.
A strong chemical used on non-living things to kill germs.
Dilute hydrogen peroxide, tincture of iodine, boric acid (any two).
Phenyl, bleaching powder, formalin, chlorine (any two).

cards.front_md: Why is a disinfectant not used on the skin?
cards.back_md: It is strong enough to harm living cells.

cards.front_md: Name three first-line defences of the body.
cards.back_md: Skin, mucus in the nose, tears (also saliva, stomach acid, cilia).

cards.front_md: What do cilia in the windpipe do?
cards.back_md: Sweep mucus with trapped germs up to the throat.

cards.front_md: What kills germs swallowed with food?
cards.back_md: The acid in the stomach.

cards.front_md: Two merits of the body's local defences?
cards.back_md: They act at once and against all kinds of germs.

cards.front_md: Three activities of the Red Cross?
cards.back_md: First aid and ambulance, disaster relief, blood banks (also training).
Fights communicable diseases, immunisation drives, research and standards.

questions.stem_md: A vaccine protects a person because it makes the body produce

options.text_md: its own antibodies and memory cells
a poison that kills the germs

questions.solution_md: A vaccine trains the body to make antibodies and memory cells — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A person who has already been exposed to dangerous germs needs protection at once. The best choice is

options.text_md: a vaccine, because it lasts longer

questions.solution_md: A serum acts at once; a vaccine needs days or weeks — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Antibiotics are useful against diseases caused by
questions.solution_md: Antibiotics act on bacteria, not on viruses — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A chemical that is strong enough to clean a hospital floor but would harm the skin is a
questions.solution_md: Strong chemicals for non-living things are disinfectants — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In the windpipe, the tiny hair-like structures that sweep mucus upward are called
questions.solution_md: Cilia beat together and sweep mucus up towards the throat — option (c).

questions.stem_md: The United Nations agency that works for the highest possible level of health for all people is the
questions.solution_md: The WHO is the health agency of the United Nations — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A girl is given a second dose of the same vaccine four weeks after the first. Her body now makes antibodies much faster because it has

options.text_md: stored ready-made antibodies from the first dose
memory cells that remember the first dose
lost all her white blood cells
destroyed the vaccine in her stomach

questions.solution_md: Memory cells formed after the first dose give a quick, strong response — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A vaccine made from weakened germs can be injected into a healthy child because the weakened germs

options.text_md: kill the white blood cells of the child
cannot cause the disease but still make the body produce antibodies
carry ready-made antibodies for the child
cause the disease but only for a very short time

questions.solution_md: A vaccine is harmless but is recognised by the body as foreign — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A newborn baby in a hospital is given a vaccine that protects against a bacterial disease of the lungs. The disease is
questions.solution_md: The vaccine given to infants against a lung disease protects against tuberculosis — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Which statement correctly separates vaccination from immunisation?

options.text_md: Vaccination is becoming immune; immunisation is giving the vaccine
Vaccination gives ready-made antibodies; immunisation gives a vaccine
Vaccination is giving the vaccine; immunisation is the person becoming immune

questions.solution_md: Vaccination is the method; immunisation is the result — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The graph shows the antibody level of a child after two doses of a vaccine. What was the highest level reached after the first dose?
questions.solution_md: The level rose to 8 by day 14 after the first dose — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Explain how a vaccine gives protection against a disease.

answer.model_answer_md: A vaccine holds **harmless germ material**, so it **cannot cause the disease**. It makes the white blood cells produce **antibodies** and **memory cells**, which respond quickly if the real germ enters later.

questions.solution_md: Harmless; antibodies and memory cells.

questions.stem_md: Differentiate between vaccination and immunisation.

answer.model_answer_md: **Vaccination** is the **giving of a vaccine** to a person. **Immunisation** is the **process of becoming immune** to a disease, which may also happen by ready-made antibodies.

questions.solution_md: Giving vaccine; becoming immune.

questions.stem_md: What is a booster dose and why is it given?

answer.model_answer_md: A **booster dose** is a **later dose** of the same vaccine. It is given so that the **memory cells** respond and the antibody level becomes **higher and lasts longer**.

questions.solution_md: Later dose; higher, longer protection.

questions.stem_md: Describe, in three steps, how a vaccine gives long-lasting protection.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The **vaccine**, made harmless, is given by injection or drops.
2. The white blood cells **make antibodies** against it, and some remain as **memory cells**.
3. If the **real germ** enters later, the memory cells make antibodies **quickly**, so the disease does not develop.

questions.solution_md: Vaccine given; antibodies and memory cells; quick response to the real germ.

questions.stem_md: Tabulate three differences between vaccination and immunisation.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Vaccination | Immunisation |
|---|---|
| **Giving** a vaccine | **Becoming immune** |
| The **method** | The **result** or whole process |
| A vaccine is **always** used | May also use **ready-made antibodies** |

questions.solution_md: Meaning; nature; use of a vaccine.

questions.stem_md: The substance that neutralises the poison made by the germs of diphtheria in a patient's body is a(n)
questions.solution_md: An antitoxin is an antibody that neutralises a toxin — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A farmer is bitten by a stray dog that may have rabies. The doctor injects ready-made antibodies at once because

options.text_md: a vaccine would cause rabies in him
a vaccine alone would need days to make the body form its own antibodies
antibiotics cannot be given to people

questions.solution_md: Ready-made antibodies act at once; a vaccine is slow — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A student keeps leftover antibiotic tablets and takes them for every fever. This is unwise because

options.text_md: many fevers are caused by viruses, and misuse makes bacteria resistant
the tablets become stronger as they age

questions.solution_md: Antibiotics do not act on viruses, and careless use gives resistant bacteria — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The first antibiotic, penicillin, was obtained from
questions.solution_md: Penicillin is made by a mould — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A patient who takes antibiotics for a long time may get loose stools, because the antibiotic also kills

options.text_md: white blood cells in the intestine
cells of the intestine wall only

questions.solution_md: Antibiotics do not distinguish useful from harmful bacteria — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Antibiotics are the right treatment for influenza.

**Reason (R):** Influenza is caused by a virus.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: The assertion is false, because antibiotics do not act on viruses. The reason is true — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Antibiotics kill bacteria.

**Reason (R):** Antibiotics act on viruses as well as on bacteria.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: The assertion is true. The reason is false: antibiotics do not act on viruses — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A serum gives protection that lasts for many years.
questions.solution_md: False. The antibodies in a serum are ready-made and fade soon; no memory cells are formed.

questions.stem_md: Give the biological term: the part of blood that holds ready-made antibodies.

answer.model_answer_md: **Serum.**

questions.solution_md: Serum.

questions.stem_md: Give reason: the protection given by a serum lasts only for a short time.

answer.model_answer_md: The antibodies are **ready-made** and are used up or removed; the body **makes no memory cells**.

questions.solution_md: No memory cells.

questions.stem_md: Give reason: a patient must finish the full course of an antibiotic even after feeling better.

answer.model_answer_md: Some **bacteria may still be alive**; they can **multiply** and may become **resistant** to the antibiotic.

questions.solution_md: Surviving bacteria become resistant.

questions.stem_md: A doctor prescribes 3 tablets a day for 10 days. A patient stops after 4 days. How many tablets are left untaken?
questions.solution_md: Full course = 3 × 10 = 30; taken = 3 × 4 = 12; left = 18.

questions.stem_md: Why is a serum given, and not a vaccine, to a person who needs protection at once?

answer.model_answer_md: A **serum** holds **ready-made antibodies**, so it **acts at once**. A vaccine makes the body build its own antibodies, which **takes days or weeks**.

questions.solution_md: Ready-made antibodies act at once; vaccine is slow.

marking_scheme.step: Serum has ready-made antibodies and acts at once

questions.stem_md: What is an antitoxin and for which kind of disease is it used?

answer.model_answer_md: An **antitoxin** is an **antibody that neutralises a poison (toxin)** made by germs. It is used in diseases in which the germs make a toxin, such as **diphtheria** or **tetanus**.

questions.solution_md: Antibody neutralising a toxin; diphtheria or tetanus.

marking_scheme.step: A disease such as diphtheria or tetanus

questions.stem_md: State what antibiotics act against and name one antibiotic.

answer.model_answer_md: Antibiotics act against **bacteria** (they kill them or stop their growth) and **not against viruses**. One antibiotic is **penicillin** (or streptomycin, tetracycline).

questions.solution_md: Bacteria; an antibiotic named.

questions.stem_md: State two harms of using antibiotics carelessly.

answer.model_answer_md: Bacteria become **resistant** to the antibiotic, and the antibiotic **kills useful bacteria** in the gut. (It may also cause an **allergy**.)

questions.solution_md: Any two harms.

questions.stem_md: State three precautions to be followed when a doctor prescribes an antibiotic.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Take it **only on the doctor's advice**, not for a cold or any fever.
2. Take the **correct dose** at the right times.
3. **Complete the full course**, even after feeling better.

questions.solution_md: Doctor's advice; correct dose; full course.

questions.stem_md: Tabulate three differences between a vaccine and an antitoxin.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Vaccine | Antitoxin |
|---|---|
| Makes the body form **its own antibodies** | Gives **ready-made antibodies** |
| **Slow** to protect | Acts **at once** |
| **Long-lasting** protection | **Short** protection |

questions.solution_md: Source of antibodies; speed; length of protection.

questions.stem_md: A boy falls and scrapes his knee. The best chemical to clean the wound is a

options.text_md: dilute antiseptic such as boric acid solution

questions.solution_md: A mild antiseptic is safe on living tissue — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A hospital washes its floors and drains with a strong chemical. Which of these is suitable for the purpose?
questions.solution_md: Bleaching powder is a disinfectant for non-living surfaces — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A disinfectant should not be applied to a cut on the skin because it

options.text_md: makes the blood clot too fast
is strong enough to harm living cells

questions.solution_md: Disinfectants are too strong for living tissue — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A nurse mixes an antiseptic concentrate with water before using it on a wound. Dilution is done to

options.text_md: give it the action of an antibiotic
make it mild enough for living tissue

questions.solution_md: Dilution makes the chemical safe for skin — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Give the biological term: a mild chemical used on living tissue to kill germs or stop their growth.

answer.model_answer_md: **Antiseptic.**

questions.solution_md: Antiseptic.

questions.stem_md: Choose the odd one out and name the category to which the other three belong: Phenyl, Bleaching powder, Formalin, Boric acid.

answer.model_answer_md: **Boric acid**; the others are **disinfectants** (boric acid is a mild antiseptic).

questions.solution_md: Boric acid is an antiseptic.

questions.stem_md: Give reason: a strong disinfectant is not applied to a wound.

answer.model_answer_md: It is **strong** and **harms the living cells** of the skin and the wound.

questions.solution_md: Harms living cells.

questions.stem_md: A nurse mixes 20 mL of antiseptic concentrate with 180 mL of water. What is the strength of the solution, in per cent of concentrate?
questions.solution_md: Volume = 20 + 180 = 200 mL; strength = 20 ÷ 200 × 100 = 10 per cent.

questions.stem_md: There are 10000 bacteria on a pair of hands. An antiseptic soap kills 99 per cent of them. How many bacteria are left?
Name one antiseptic and one disinfectant, and state where each is used.

answer.model_answer_md: **Boric acid** (or dilute hydrogen peroxide) is an **antiseptic**, used on **wounds and skin**. **Bleaching powder** (or phenyl) is a **disinfectant**, used on **floors and drains**.

questions.solution_md: Antiseptic and use; disinfectant and use.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between an antiseptic and a disinfectant on the basis of strength and place of use.

answer.model_answer_md: An **antiseptic** is **mild** and is used on **living tissue**. A **disinfectant** is **strong** and is used on **non-living things** such as floors and drains.

questions.solution_md: Mild, living tissue; strong, non-living things.

questions.stem_md: State where each of these is used: (i) an antiseptic, (ii) a disinfectant, (iii) an antibiotic.

wash the surface and contain an enzyme that kills bacteria

questions.solution_md: Stomach acid kills most swallowed germs — option (a).

options.text_md: carry the germs to the stomach
trap dust and germs before they reach the lungs

questions.solution_md: Hairs and sticky mucus trap particles — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A germ trapped in the mucus lining the windpipe is most likely to

options.text_md: be swept up to the throat and swallowed or coughed out
be carried down to the lungs by the cilia
be killed at once by the mucus alone
enter the blood through the mucus

questions.solution_md: Cilia sweep the mucus upward — option (a).

They act at once against many kinds of germs
They work only after a person has fallen ill

questions.solution_md: First-line defences are immediate and general — option (c).

**Assertion (A):** Tears protect the eye from infection.

**Reason (R):** Tears contain water and salts.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but the water and salts do not explain the protection, which is due to the enzyme in tears and the washing action — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Give the biological term: the sticky fluid in the nose and windpipe that traps dust and germs.

answer.model_answer_md: **Mucus.**

questions.solution_md: Mucus.

questions.stem_md: Choose the odd one out and name the category to which the other three belong: Skin, Tears, Mucus, Serum.

answer.model_answer_md: **Serum**; the others are **first-line defences of the body** (serum holds ready-made antibodies).

questions.solution_md: Serum is not a first-line defence.

questions.stem_md: Give reason: breathing through the nose is healthier than breathing through the mouth.

answer.model_answer_md: The **hairs and mucus** in the nose **trap dust and germs**, so the air that reaches the lungs is cleaner.

questions.solution_md: Nose traps dust and germs.

questions.stem_md: A person breathes in 1000 particles of dust and germs. The mucus in the nose traps 950 of them. How many particles get past the nose?
A person breathes in 1000 particles. The nose traps 950 of them. The windpipe then traps 80 per cent of the particles that got past the nose. How many particles reach the lungs?
questions.solution_md: Past the nose = 1000 − 950 = 50; trapped in the windpipe = 50 × 80 ÷ 100 = 40; reach the lungs = 50 − 40 = 10.

questions.stem_md: State two ways in which the skin protects the body from germs.

answer.model_answer_md: The **horny layer** is a **tough, waterproof barrier** that germs cannot easily cross. The **oil and sweat** on its surface make it **unfriendly to germs**.

questions.solution_md: Tough barrier; oil and sweat.

questions.stem_md: Name two first-line defences in the nose and windpipe and state the role of each.

answer.model_answer_md: **Mucus** (with hairs in the nose) **traps dust and germs**. **Cilia** in the windpipe **sweep the mucus upward** to the throat.

questions.solution_md: Mucus traps; cilia sweep.

questions.stem_md: State how (i) tears and (ii) the stomach acid protect the body.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) **Tears** wash the eye and contain an **enzyme that kills bacteria**. (ii) The **acid in the stomach kills** most germs that are swallowed with food and water.

questions.solution_md: Tears wash and kill; acid kills swallowed germs.

questions.stem_md: Describe how the skin, the mucus in the nose and the tears help to keep germs out of the body.

answer.model_answer_md: The **skin** is a **tough barrier** that germs cannot cross. The **mucus** in the nose **traps dust and germs**. **Tears** wash the eye and hold an **enzyme that kills bacteria**.

questions.solution_md: Skin barrier; mucus traps; tears wash and kill.

questions.stem_md: State three merits of the first-line defences of the body.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. They are **always in place** and act **at once**.
2. They act against **all kinds of germs**, not just one kind.
3. They are **natural**: no injection or medicine is needed. (They also stop most germs from getting in.)

questions.solution_md: Immediate; general; natural.

questions.stem_md:
In a school clinic a nurse mixes 20 mL of an antiseptic concentrate with 180 mL of clean water to clean a student's scraped elbow. The floor of the clinic is washed with a stronger chemical.

(a) Calculate the volume of the solution and its strength in per cent. [2]

(b) Explain why the concentrate is diluted before it is used on the elbow. [2]

(c) Name one disinfectant and state why it is not used on the skin. [2]

(d) Draw a neat, labelled diagram of a first-aid box showing four items. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Volume = 20 + 180 = **200 mL**; strength = 20 ÷ 200 × 100 = **10 per cent**.

**(b)** The concentrate is **strong**; diluted, it is **mild enough** not to harm the **living cells** of the skin, but still kills germs.

**(c)** **Bleaching powder** (or phenyl); it is **too strong** and would **damage living tissue**.

**(d)** A **box** with a lid showing, for example, an **antiseptic bottle**, **cotton wool**, a **bandage** and **adhesive plasters**; four labels.

questions.solution_md: 200 mL, 10 per cent; dilution makes it mild; a disinfectant, too strong; labelled first-aid box.

questions.stem_md:
A doctor prescribes 3 antibiotic tablets a day for 10 days to a boy with a bacterial throat infection. He feels better and stops after 4 days. Later, his brother with a cold asks for the same tablets.

(a) Calculate the number of tablets in the full course and the percentage of the course left untaken. [2]

(b) Explain why the full course should be completed. [2]

(c) Explain why the tablets will not help the brother's cold. [2]

(d) Draw a neat flow diagram showing how careless use of an antibiotic can lead to resistant bacteria, with four labelled steps. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** Full course = 3 × 10 = **30 tablets**; left = 18 ÷ 30 × 100 = **60 per cent**.

**(b)** Some **bacteria may still be alive**; they can **multiply** and may become **resistant**.

**(c)** A cold is caused by a **virus**, and antibiotics **do not act on viruses**.

**(d)** **Antibiotic stopped early** → **some bacteria survive** → **they multiply** → **a resistant infection**; four labelled steps joined by arrows.

questions.solution_md: 30 tablets, 60 per cent left; survivors multiply and may become resistant; a cold is viral; flow diagram.

marking_scheme.step: Cold is caused by a virus
Antibiotics do not act on viruses

questions.stem_md:
A farmer is bitten by a stray dog that may have rabies. At the hospital he is given a liquid that holds ready-made antibodies, as well as a vaccine.

(a) Name the liquid and state where its antibodies may come from. [2]

(b) Explain why ready-made antibodies are given in addition to the vaccine. [2]

(c) Explain why the protection given by the liquid does not last long. [2]

(d) Draw a neat flow diagram showing how a serum may be prepared from an animal, with four labelled steps. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** A **serum**; the antibodies come from an **immunised animal** such as a horse (or from a recovered person).

**(b)** The serum **acts at once**, while the vaccine takes **days or weeks** to make the body form its own antibodies.

**(c)** The antibodies are **ready-made** and fade soon; the body **forms no memory cells**.

**(d)** **Harmless dose of germ or toxin injected into a horse** → **horse makes antibodies** → **blood collected** → **serum separated and purified**; four labelled steps joined by arrows.

questions.solution_md: Serum, from an immunised animal; acts at once; no memory cells; flow diagram.

questions.stem_md:
After an earthquake, a relief team of the Red Cross gives 2 blankets to each of 480 families. A health agency of the United Nations sends experts to check the drinking water and to prevent an outbreak of disease.

(a) Calculate the number of blankets needed. [2]

(b) State two other activities of the Red Cross. [2]

(c) Name the agency of the United Nations and state three of its major activities. [3]

(d) Draw the emblem of the Red Cross and label the colour of the cross and the colour of the background. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** 480 × 2 = **960 blankets**.

**(b)** **First aid and ambulance service**, **blood donation camps and blood banks**, training in first aid (any two).

**(c)** The **World Health Organization (WHO)**. It **fights communicable diseases** (immunisation drives), **responds to epidemics**, does **research**, sets **standards** for medicines and food, **trains health workers** (any three).

**(d)** A **red cross** on a **white background**, with both colours labelled.

questions.solution_md: 960 blankets; two Red Cross activities; WHO and three activities; emblem.

marking_scheme.step: Colour of cross and of background
